program_plain: World: a 64x64 lattice of cells (wrap-around edges, 8 neighbours each). Cells have 2 types (cooperator, defector; half each at random). Rules each step: every cell plays a prisoner's dilemma with its 8 neighbours and itself (temptation 1.2, sucker payoff 0); then every cell copies the type of the highest-scoring cell in its neighbourhood.
model_family: Evolutionary game theory on a lattice / deterministic synchronous cellular automaton (spatial prisoner's dilemma, imitate-the-best)
standard_name: Nowak-May spatial prisoner's dilemma (spatial reciprocity); static regime 1<b<9/5 (Moore neighbourhood with self-interaction)

full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** The rule system is the Nowak–May spatial prisoner's dilemma, and it is described there. I could not read the 1993 paper's text, so my confidence on the exact match is medium. The reasoning is below.

**1. Model family.** This is evolutionary game theory on a lattice, run as a deterministic synchronous cellular automaton. The standard name is the "Nowak–May spatial prisoner's dilemma" (spatial reciprocity, imitate-the-best).
- Players are unconditional C or D.
- Payoffs are R=1, S=P=0, T=b, with b=1.2 or 1.3 here.
- Each cell plays its 8 Moore neighbours plus itself.
- Each cell then copies the best scorer in its 3×3 neighbourhood.
- One source describes this as a deterministic model equivalent to a two-state cellular automaton.
- Another confirms that Nowak and May's simulations are an 8+1 neighbourhood, because every player also plays herself.

**2. The specific behaviour and its sources.**
- **What I think was observed.** b=1.2 and 1.3 both fall below the chaotic regime, which is 9/5<b<2 with self-interaction. The run converges to a mostly frozen, one-strategy-dominated state with little ongoing activity. I read "one type fills most of the lattice" as dominance by one strategy, not extinction of the other. That reading is my inference from the metrics.
- **Earliest source.** Nowak & May (1992), "Evolutionary games and spatial chaos", Nature 359, 826–829. Nature's page lists it as published 29 October 1992, DOI 10.1038/359826a0. The fuller treatment is Nowak & May (1993), "The spatial dilemmas of evolution", Int. J. Bifurcation Chaos 3, 35–78. Its title and venue are confirmed only through other papers' reference lists.
- **What the literature says about b below 9/5.**
  - In the Szabó–Fáth review, outside the chaotic region the strategy frequencies and their limit values depend on the initial configuration.
  - Szabó & Tőke (1998) say that in the Nowak–May deterministic model, isolated gangs with fixed positions can occur if 1 < b < 4/3. Both b=1.2 and b=1.3 fall in this range. The authors note that the gangs' density depends on the initial state.
  - A later study of the same model reports that for b < 9/5 the system develops relatively static web-like structures of defectors. That run started from 10% cooperators, not 50%.
- **Related result.** Another paper on this model, with the same regime classification, reports that for b=1.1 all updating schemes converged to a static configuration, with defectors surrounded by cooperators. That run used fixed boundaries and a 50% start.
- **Review.** Szabó & Fáth (2007), "Evolutionary games on graphs", Physics Reports 446, 97–216. It is confirmed as an Elsevier ScienceDirect entry with Szabó and Fáth as authors, and an arXiv version exists (cond-mat/0607344). Its section 6.5 covers this synchronous-update model.

**3. Why the verdict is KNOWN and not a variant.** The rules are identical to the original. The parameters sit in the documented sub-chaotic, static regime, where cooperators dominate and defectors persist only as fixed clusters.
- Szabó–Tőke's fixed-gang range, 1<b<4/3, covers both b=1.2 and b=1.3.
- Nowak–May describe the same sub-regimes, with thresholds at 9/8, 8/7, 7/6, 6/5, 5/4 and 4/3. I saw the threshold ladder in a related paper's table (arXiv cond-mat/0504782), not in Nowak–May's text.

**4. Caveats and confidence.**
- I did not find a source that reports, for exactly b=1.2 or 1.3 with a 50% random start on a 64×64 torus, which strategy fills the lattice. That depends on the initial condition. My reading that cooperators dominate comes from the C-cluster and D-gang picture, not from a direct citation.
- "Activity rising" is odd given a trend value of −5.0. I read it as activity falling to a frozen state. The cited sources do not report activity-trend metrics.
- The 1993 paper (the detailed sub-regime classification) I confirmed only through other papers' reference lists, not by reading it.
